title: What Are Learning Strategies? Core Categories Explained
brief: Define the term 'strategy' using the source's own wording: 'a tool, plan, or method used for accomplishing a task.' Then distinguish the three main categories the source identifies—cognitive, metacognitive, and social/affective strategies—drawing on the definitions provided in Reading B (Cohen). Cognitive strategies include memorizing and manipulating target language structures; metacognitive strategies involve managing and supervising strategy use; social strategies include cooperating with other learners and seeking to interact with native speakers. Close by noting the source's point that strategies are mostly 'invisible' mental processes, so teachers must analyze and infer what strategies are at work rather than observe them directly.

title: Cognitive Strategies: Tools for Processing and Remembering Language
brief: Focus entirely on cognitive strategies as described in the source. Draw on Reading A (Beckman) to explain that cognitive strategies are used to perform academic tasks and that successful learners use numerous strategies, often in combination. List and explain concrete examples from the source: visualization, verbalization, making associations, chunking, questioning, scanning, underlining, accessing cues, using mnemonics, sounding out words, and self-checking and monitoring. Use the source's specific mnemonic example (PLAN: Pay attention to the prompt, List main ideas, Add supporting ideas, Number your ideas) to illustrate how a cognitive strategy can be made concrete and teachable. Emphasize the source's point that these strategies are especially effective when used in combinations rather than in isolation.

title: Metacognitive Strategies: Helping Learners Think About Their Own Learning
brief: Explain metacognition using the source's definition: 'global understanding of thinking or mental processes that enables learners to recognize, monitor, and organize those processes in themselves.' Draw on both readings to describe what metacognitive strategy use looks like in practice—self-diagnosing strengths and weaknesses, monitoring performance, evaluating the effectiveness of a strategy after use, and transferring successful strategies to new contexts. Use the four-stage problem-solving process from Reading B (Chamot and O'Malley's framework: Planning, Monitoring, Problem Solving, Evaluation) as a concrete classroom-ready example of how metacognitive strategy use can be structured. Connect this to the source's description of the 'independent, strategic learner' who asks clarifying questions, checks and monitors work, and sets personal goals.

title: Social Strategies: Learning With and From Others
brief: Cover social strategies as defined in Reading B: strategies for enhancing learning through cooperating with other learners and seeking to interact with native speakers. Draw on the classroom example from the video answer key, which describes the teacher strategically forming student pairs and groups for support and use of shared knowledge, and giving each group a different topic so students had to communicate results to the rest of the class. Include the peer tutoring model from Reading B as a further example of social strategy use: pairing students of different backgrounds for mutual tutoring, alternating learner and teacher roles, and exchanging suggestions about strategies they use. Note the source's point that students in a social learning environment felt comfortable contributing to their own and other groups' reports and connected personal experiences to class content.

title: Building Strategy Training Into Normal Lessons
brief: Explain how strategy instruction should be embedded inside regular classroom teaching rather than treated as a separate subject, drawing directly on Reading A's statement that 'effective strategy instruction is an integral part of classroom instruction, regardless of the content being taught; it is not an additional subject.' Present the step-by-step teaching sequence from Reading A: describe the strategy and its purpose, model its use, provide assisted practice with feedback, promote student self-monitoring and evaluation, and encourage transfer to new situations. Supplement with the Strategies-Based Instruction (SBI) approach from Reading B, detailing what teachers do in a typical SBI classroom: describing and modeling strategies, eliciting examples from students, leading discussions, encouraging experimentation, and integrating strategies explicitly and implicitly into everyday class materials. Include the source's note that written reminders for learning strategies posted on classroom walls can help students with the learning process.

title: Helping Learners Build Strategies Between Classes
brief: Address how teachers can support learner strategy use outside the classroom, drawing on the source's action-plan section and the goals of strategy training listed in Reading B. Cover the source's goals of helping learners self-diagnose their strengths and weaknesses, become aware of what helps them learn most efficiently, experiment with familiar and unfamiliar strategies, and transfer successful strategies to new learning contexts. Use the source's concrete suggestions from the action-plan steps: creating a trusting classroom atmosphere that encourages risk-taking, building student confidence, activating schema, and helping students transfer skills to appropriate language use outside class (such as content classes taught in English, understanding music and movies, or talking with foreigners). Close with the source's description of what happens when learners become strategic: they trust their minds, know there is more than one right way to do things, develop a personal study process, and become more autonomous self-teachers who can continue learning after they leave the language classroom.
